_note: Narration keyed by beat id. Written to COMPLEMENT the on-screen copy, never to read it aloud — a viewer who can see 'Two samples' does not need to be told it. Stage 9 register: a senior systems architect addressing professional engineering peers. Measured, data-heavy, no commercial enthusiasm.
r1-hook: Every fader on this surface is a request. None of them touches audio.
r1-problem: Forty channels of live transients, summed onto one bus. In fixed-point arithmetic that is where the arguments about headroom start.
r1-edge: Conversion happens at the rear panel. From there inward, the console is arithmetic.
r1-hdia: The first gain stage is a true instrumentation amplifier — the topology built to hold a small difference steady while everything around it is noisy.
r1-demo-hdia: Interference arrives on both legs equally. The difference amplifier keeps what differs and discards what matches, before conversion.
r1-ein: Minus one hundred and twenty-eight dBu of equivalent input noise, with thirty-two dBu of headroom above it.
r1-adc: Thirty-two-bit conversion at ninety-six kilohertz, feeding straight into the engine.
r1-fpga: The summing runs in a field-programmable gate array. Not a fixed-point DSP chip — an array of gates configured to do this one job in parallel.
r1-demo-sum: Forty-two bits carry amplitude. Twelve are reserved above it. Whatever you sum, the bus does not run out of room.
r1-latency: Two samples through the engine. Twenty-point-eight microseconds. Half a millisecond analog to analog.
r1-matrix: Forty-four input channels, twenty-two flexible buses, thirty-two in total.
r1-two: Sixteen faders or twenty-four. The engine behind them is the same one.
r2-hook: The engineer stays where the engineer needs to be. The copper does not have to follow.
r2-replace: One network run, carrying what a multicore carried, over infrastructure the building already has.
r2-dante: Sixty-four channels in and sixty-four out are part of every Sonicview. Not a card, not an upgrade path.
r2-redundant: Primary and secondary. The same audio, down two physically separate networks, simultaneously.
r2-demo-red: Cut one path and nothing is heard to happen. The receiver reconstructs from the other stream with no sample lost. It is a path that stopped being used.
r2-sb16d: This is not a mixer. It is the console's input stage, relocated to where the microphones already are.
r2-parity: The same Class One HDIA preamps as the console. Moving an input changes nothing about it.
r2-scale: More inputs means another box on the same network. The console does not change.
r2-remote: Gain, phantom power and pad, set from the desk while the show is running. Nobody walks back to stage — which is a safety property before it is a convenience.
r2-demo-afv: A camera tally closes a contact. The fader calculates its own rise, hold and fall, and moves.
r2-automation: Ember-plus for newsroom automation. N-MOS for discovery and connection management. S-N-M-P for monitoring.
r2-cards: Two expansion bays, and a second power supply for the rooms where silence is the failure.
r3-hook: Three screens, one engine, and one person who has to reach all of it.
r3-view: Channel strip, module, individual. The operator picks the view that matches the task rather than the one the desk insists on.
r3-demo-recall: A scene recall is one state change, not twenty-five moves. Every fader departs together and arrives together.
r3-faders: One hundred millimetre motorised faders, mapped to layers the engineer defines.
r3-spill: A group opened out across the surface, then folded away again.
r3-keys: Eighteen assignable keys with colour feedback. Tap tempo, mute groups, snapshot state.
r3-curve: The processing is arithmetic, but the operator has to see it. Curves redraw as they are edited.
r3-geq: Thirty-one-band graphic EQ and a real-time analyser, on every one of the twenty-two buses.
r3-mtr32: Thirty-two tracks direct to S-D card. The write file closes every sixty seconds, so a power fault costs a minute, not a session.
r3-usb: Thirty-two in and thirty-two out to the computer, at the same time.
r3-air: Broadcast, remote production, live installation. The requirement keeps its shape.
p1-cold: A mixing console used to be a room full of copper with a surface on top. This one is a computation node that happens to have faders.
p1-problem: Consider what a live bus actually has to survive. Forty channels of transient material, arriving together, summed in real time, with no opportunity to try again.
p1-edge: Every analog input is converted at the physical boundary of the chassis. Past that point there is no analog signal path left to protect — which changes what the rest of the design has to worry about.
p1-hdia: The first gain stage is a true instrumentation amplifier. High input impedance, high common-mode rejection, and discrete components sized so the supply can deliver current when a transient asks for it.
p1-demo-hdia: An instrumentation amplifier amplifies the difference between two inputs and rejects what is common to both. Interference induced on a cable run arrives on both legs equally, so it subtracts to nothing while the signal survives.
p1-ein: Equivalent input noise of minus one hundred and twenty-eight dBu, with a maximum input level of plus thirty-two dBu.
p1-adc: The preamps feed the converters directly. Thirty-two-bit analog to digital, twenty-four-bit back out, at ninety-six kilohertz throughout.
p1-fpga: The mixing engine is a field-programmable gate array rather than a fixed-point DSP chip. That is a difference in kind: an array of gates configured to perform this specific arithmetic, in parallel, every sample.
p1-demo-sum: Fifty-four bits, allocated deliberately: forty-two carry amplitude, twelve are held above as headroom. The consequence is that the internal bus cannot be clipped, however many channels are summed into it.
p1-headroom: Twelve bits of margin, reserved and never spent.
p1-latency: Two samples through the engine. At ninety-six kilohertz that is twenty-point-eight microseconds — short enough that in-ear monitoring stays phase-coherent.
p1-roundtrip: Analog in to analog out, through conversion, processing and conversion again: half a millisecond.
p1-channels: Forty-four input channels, forty mono and two stereo, plus four effect returns. Twenty-two flexible buses that can be subgroups, auxiliaries or matrices, alongside the main pair and four effect sends.
p1-dsp: Every channel gets delay, phase, trim, a high-pass filter, gating, parametric EQ and compression. Every bus gets a graphic EQ, an analyser, compression and delay. None of it is a shared pool that runs out.
p1-segregation: The graphical operating system is separated from the engine. If the interface halts, the gate array keeps passing audio, keeps clocking the network, and keeps processing.
p1-sixteen: Sixteen faders, two screens, thirteen kilograms.
p1-bridge: Twenty-four faders, three screens, the same forty-four channels underneath.
p2-cold: Part two. Once conversion happens at the edge, the question stops being how much copper you can pull and starts being where you put the converters.
p2-aoip: Audio over a network is not a compression of the old idea. Channels become streams, patching becomes routing, and a single cable stops caring how many channels it carries.
p2-dante: Sixty-four channels in and sixty-four out, at forty-eight kilohertz. Thirty-two each way at ninety-six. On every model, from power-on.
p2-redundant: Two physically separate networks carrying identical streams. Not a failover that takes a moment — both are live, all the time.
p2-demo-red: The receiver is already holding both. Sever one and it continues from the other with no sample lost and no interruption to hear. The failure is a maintenance ticket, not a broadcast event.
p2-sb16d: The SB-sixteen-D is not a mixer, and describing it as one misses what it is for. It is the console's input stage, moved to the stage end.
p2-sbio: Sixteen microphone and line inputs, sixteen line outputs, the same Class One HDIA preamps and the same thirty-two-bit conversion as the console itself.
p2-chassis: Three rack units, four and a half kilograms, built to survive a load-in rather than only an installation.
p2-scale: When the input count grows, a second box joins the same network. Nothing about the console changes.
p2-remote: Preamp gain, forty-eight-volt phantom power and pad, per channel, set from the desk while the programme is running — or from anywhere else on the network.
p2-gpio: Eight general-purpose inputs and eight outputs, expanding to sixteen each way alongside the console.
p2-demo-afv: The video switcher closes a contact. The console reads it as a trigger and computes the fader move itself, to defined rise, hold and fall times. The operator is not in the loop, which is the point.
p2-automix: In unscripted discussion the auto mixer calculates priority and weight continuously, holding down the microphones nobody is using.
p2-protocols: Ember-plus lets a newsroom automation system drive faders and mutes directly. N-MOS handles discovery and connection management. S-N-M-P reports health to whatever already monitors the building.
p2-st2110: The IF-S-T-twenty-one-ten card takes the console into an IP video fabric — sixty-four channels each way, with the discovery and connection management a broadcast controller expects.
p2-cards: AES-EBU, analog outputs, additional Dante, MADI over coaxial and optical. The bay decides what the console is for.
p2-dp: The dual-power models add a four-pin DC inlet alongside the mains supply. A fault at the wall does not become a fault on air.
p3-cold: Part three. Everything established so far still has to be operated by one person, usually under time pressure, often by somebody who is not an audio engineer.
p3-view: The VIEW system offers three ways of looking at the same console. Channel strip for comparison across adjacent inputs, module for everything happening to one, individual for a layout the engineer defines.
p3-strip: Eight channels side by side — the reading an analog desk gives you for free, reconstructed deliberately.
p3-module: One channel, three processing blocks, nothing else competing for the screen.
p3-individual: And a layout built around how one particular room actually works.
p3-demo-recall: A snapshot recall is a single state change. Every fader leaves at once and arrives at once, whatever distance each has to travel, and none of them overshoots.
p3-faders: One hundred millimetre motorised faders across custom layers, with sends-on-fader and DCA spill.
p3-userkeys: Eighteen assignable keys with full-colour feedback, so the functions that matter tonight are under the hand rather than three menus away.
p3-workflow: What changes on the day is the shape of the room: what has to be carried in, what stays racked, and how long it takes to be ready.
p3-mtr32: Thirty-two tracks recorded directly to an S-D card, with no computer in the path. The write file is closed every sixty seconds, so an abrupt power loss costs a minute.
p3-usb: Thirty-two channels in and thirty-two out over USB, simultaneously, for the sessions that do want a computer.
p3-slots: A recorder in one bay and a broadcast transport in the other, at the same time.
p3-radio: A working broadcast facility, where the schedule does not stop for an installation and the operators are presenters rather than engineers.
p3-campus: A conference facility with a genuinely complex routing requirement and a rota of staff who were never going to be trained as audio engineers. Complex behind, simple in front.
p3-remote: And remote production, where the console is assembled, used and struck inside a day.
p3-system: Console, stagebox, expansion cards, network. The parts were designed against each other.
p3-validate: Architect the system before you specify the hardware. Shivansh Electronics is TASCAM's authorized partner for system design, protocol matching and infrastructure planning across India.
_outro: Talk to the team about your facility.
